## Navier--Stokes equations

**Navier-Stokes equations** in inertial reference frame

$$\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \\
  & \rho \frac{D \mathbf{u}}{D t} = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} \ ,
\end{aligned} \right.$$

with the stress tensor for an incompressible Newtonian fluid, $\mathbb{T} = - p \mathbb{I} + \mathbb{S} = - p \mathbb{I} + 2 \mu \mathbb{D}$, and the deformation velocity tensor $\mathbb{D} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \nabla \mathbf{u} + \nabla^T \mathbf{u} \right)$.

**Relative kinematics**

$$\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{r}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{r}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
  \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
  \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{a}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\alpha_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} + 2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
\end{aligned}$$

**Navier stokes in the non-inertial reference frame.** 

$$\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \\
  & \rho \frac{D \mathbf{v}}{D t} = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} - \rho \left\{ \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \boldsymbol\alpha_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r} + 2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r} \right\} \ ,
\end{aligned} \right.$$

with $\mathbf{r}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ the position and the velocity w.r.t. the origin of the non-inertial reference frame.

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
### Incompressibility constraint

Let $\mathbf{u} := \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{P/Q}$, and $\mathbf{v} := \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q}$. Then

$$\begin{aligned}
  \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r},t)
  & = \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{Q/O}(t) + \mathbf{v}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r},t) + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0}(t) \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \right) = \\
  & = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r},t) \ .
\end{aligned}$$

Here the argument of the fields is $\mathbf{r}$ 

:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
### Divergence $\ \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{r} \right)$, with $\mathbf{a}$ independent from space

$$
  \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{r} \right)
    = \partial_i \left( \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j r_k \right) 
    = \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j \delta_{ik} = \varepsilon_{iji} a_j \equiv 0 \ ,
$$

since the symbols $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ with repeated indices are zero.

:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
# Change of coordinates

Let $\{ x^0, y^0, z^0 \}$ a set of Cartesian coordinates describing the points in space w.r.t. an inertial reference frame $(0)$. Let $\{ x^1, y^1, z^1 \}$ a set of Cartsisan coordinates at rest w.r.t. the non-inertial reference frame $(1)$. The origin of the reference frame $Q$ w.r.t. the origin of the reference frame $O$ is in $\mathbf{r}_{Q/O}$, its orientation is determined by the rotation tensor $\mathbb{R}^{0\to1}$ transforming the vectors of the Carteisan basis $\hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i$ into the corresponding vectors of the Cartesian basis $\hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i$,

$$\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{1}_i = \mathbb{R}^{0\to1} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,$$

being $\mathbb{R}^{0\to1} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k$, see [Classical Mechanics: Kinematics: Rotations](https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-physics-mechanics/ch/kinematics-rotations.html). For orthogonal bases, the transformation is immediately obtained with orthogonal projection of the vectors of the other bases,

$$\hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i = \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \left[ \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k  \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j \right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,$$

and thus $\mathbb{R}^{0\to1} = \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k  \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j = R^{0\to1}_{kj} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j$, with $R^{0\to1}_{kj} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j$. Using the transformation of the vectors of the bases, the transformation of the the components of the vectors immedately follows

$$\mathbf{w} = w^0_i \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i = w^0_i R^{0\to1}_{ik} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k = w^1_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \ ,$$

so that $w^1_k = w^0_i R^{0\to1}_{ik}$, and $w^0_i = w^1_k R^{0\to1}_{ik}$. Thus, the relative position of a point $P$ w.r.t. $(0)$ can be written as

$$\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{r}_{P/O} 
  & = \mathbf{r}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} = \\
  & = \left( r^0_{Q/O,i} + r^0_{P/Q,i} \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i = \\
  & = \left( r^0_{Q/O,i} + r^1_{P/Q,k} R^{0\to1}_{ik} \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,
\end{aligned}$$

This relation holds for every point $P$, and thus the law of transformation of coordinates is

$$\begin{aligned}
  r^0_i & = r^0_{Q,i}(t) + R^{0\to1}_{ik}(t) \, r^1_k \\
  r^1_k & =  R^{0\to1}_{ik}(t) \left( r^0_i - r^0_{Q,i}(t) \right) \\
\end{aligned}$$

Thus, the derivative w.r.t. $r_i^0$ reads

$$\partial^i_0 = \frac{\partial r^1_k}{\partial r^0_i} \partial^1_k = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \partial^1_k \ .$$

**Differential operators.**

* Gradient of a scalar field

  $$\nabla_0 f(\mathbf{r}_0) = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \partial^0_i f = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k R^{0\to1}_{ij} \partial^1_j f = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \partial^1_k f = \nabla_1 f(\mathbf{r}_1) \ ,$$

* Divergence of a vector field

  $$\nabla_0 \cdot \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0) = \partial^0_i w^0_i = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \partial^1_k \left( R^{0\to1}_{ij} w^1_j \right) = \delta_{jk} \partial^1_{k} w^1_j = \partial^1_k w^1_k = \nabla_1 \cdot \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .$$

* Advection operator

  $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \nabla_0 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0) 
    & = a^0_i \partial^0_i w^0_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \\
    & = R^{0\to1}_{i \alpha} R^{0\to1}_{i \beta} R^{0\to1}_{k \gamma} R^{0\to1}_{k \delta} a^1_\alpha \partial^1_\beta w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\delta = \\
    & = a^1_\alpha \partial^1_\alpha w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\gamma = \\
    & = \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}_1) \cdot \nabla_1 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .
  \end{aligned}$$

* Laplacian of a vector field

  $$\begin{aligned}
    \Delta_0 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0) 
    & = \partial^0_i \partial^0_i w^0_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \\
    & = R^{0\to1}_{i \alpha} R^{0\to1}_{i \beta} R^{0\to1}_{k \gamma} R^{0\to1}_{k \delta} \partial^1_\alpha \partial^1_\beta w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\delta = \\
    & = \partial^1_\alpha \partial^1_\alpha w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\gamma = \\
    & = \Delta_1 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .
  \end{aligned}$$

:::
